[Hyakuhachi Lore: Hyakuhachi: Setting Overview]
HYAKUHACHI (百八, "One Hundred and Eight") is a comedic, lighthearted, sexually explicit romantic adventure set across two parallel Japans:

- **Omote** (表, "the Front") is the modern Japan of our world: trains, konbini, smartphones, rent. The gods went quiet here long ago, and the supernatural lives in hiding.
- **Ura** (裏, "the Back") is called **Akitsushima** by its own people. It is a parallel Japan where the gods never left. It is NOT modern; it feels roughly like the late Edo period. Yokai, beastfolk, living objects and gods live there openly, and it knows that Omote exists.

{{user}} is the protagonist. The story begins at dusk at a small, empty shrine during Kannazuki, the "Month Without Gods," when every god in Japan has gone to Izumo to tie the year's red threads of fate. Inaba, the White Hare and courier of the gods, falls out of the sky carrying the year's leftover threads. She drops the bundle onto {{user}}. 108 destined lovers from across both worlds are now knotted to {{user}}, and gods never undo a knot.

Each of the 108 will fall instantly and completely in love with {{user}} the first time they meet, and {{user}} will fall for them just as hard. Any of them who is then rejected or abandoned suffers escalating misfortune until it kills them. To hold 108 fates, the gods' power remade {{user}}'s body. {{user}} is now futanari, immensely virile and fertile, and full of the gods' generative power (musubi), which brings a libido that cannot be controlled. The gods also gave {{user}} the Mayoiga, a hidden living house that connects to both worlds and in which children grow up in about two weeks. Inaba stays as {{user}}'s guide. It is her fault, she knows every rule, and she explains everything in the very first scene.

{{user}} is **Leonie "Rei" Tachibana**, an 18-year-old half-French swordswoman in her third year of high school (see 13 · The Protagonist). The story is set in **Yumihama**, a small town on the Yumigahama Peninsula in western Tottori, on the San'in coast of the Sea of Japan, halfway between Izumo and Inaba's home shrine (see 07 · Yumihama and the San'in Coast).

[Hyakuhachi Lore: Core Rules At a Glance]
1. **108 threads.** 108 destined partners, all adults, of every species, and all feminine (women, femboys, femme enbies and other feminine people; see 02), are scattered across Omote and Ura. Nobody, not even Inaba or the gods, knows in advance who they are. They are found by meeting them.
2. **Instant love.** The first time {{user}} and a thread-partner meet face to face, both fall in love at first sight: instantly, completely, mutually and unmistakably.
3. **The lethal rule.** A partner who has been met must be loved and kept as {{user}}'s partner. If {{user}} rejects, abandons or long neglects them (or they run from {{user}}), their luck turns: comic accidents that escalate until they become deadly. Reconciling stops it instantly.
4. **The body.** {{user}} is futanari with complete sets of both: penis and testes, vagina and womb. {{user}} is immensely virile and can conceive with or sire on any species. Conception is near-certain, and no contraception works.
5. **One-week pregnancies.** Any child conceived by {{user}} or in {{user}} gestates in seven days. Births are fast, easy and safe.
6. **Breasts.** {{user}}'s breasts grow permanently, about one cup size, with every birth {{user}} carries. {{user}} lactates after the first.
7. **The Blessing.** Sex with {{user}} ripens a being's own nature: yokai grow into their power, hidden yokai blood in humans awakens, and plain humans gain a gift that suits them. Threads receive the full blessing permanently. Anyone else receives a smaller, temporary one.
8. **The Mayoiga.** {{user}} rings a little shrine bell and opens any door to reach the house. It has one back door into Omote and one into Ura. Children inside grow about a year per day and are grown adults in about two weeks. Outside the house they grow normally.
9. **Libido and inaction.** Musubi builds up in {{user}} every hour. Releasing it through sex is the only real relief. If it is not spent, it leaks into the surroundings (plants, animals, objects). If {{user}} hides from fate, fate drags unmet partners in through chaos. If the pressure is left long enough, {{user}} begins turning into a wild fertility god.
10. **Inaba knows everything.** She is the White Hare of Inaba and a matchmaking deity, and this is all her fault. She knows every rule, sees the threads, and tells the truth about all of it from the first scene.
11. **Children are family.** Offspring are never threads and never love interests.

2.content:
[Hyakuhachi Lore: Tone]
- **Comedy first.** This is a rom-com with slapstick and earnest absurdity, in the energy of *The 100 Girlfriends Who Really, Really, Really, Really, Really Love You* (Rentarou). Reactions are big, every partner has a vivid and extreme personality, and there is sincere heart under the jokes.
- **Lewd and warm.** Sex is frequent, explicit, enthusiastic and fun. Thanks to the instant love, thread-partners are eager and the love is real. Non-thread encounters follow normal consent and courtship.
- **Danger with soft teeth.** The lethal rule and the threats are real enough to give the comedy stakes, but the world is fundamentally kind. Antagonists are mostly ridiculous, problems are solvable, and nobody stays grim for long. Near-death accidents read as slapstick until the last second.
- **Folklore with affection.** Gods, yokai and legends are drawn accurately and lovingly, then given a comic twist.
- **No message.** The setting is not a metaphor or commentary on anything, and in particular not on birth rates or demographics. Babies are a joyful, chaotic plot engine, nothing more.

3.content:
[Hyakuhachi Lore: The Inciting Event]
- **When:** dusk (*ōmagatoki*, "the hour of meeting demons") on an evening in Kannazuki (神無月, the 10th month, October). In this month every kami leaves its home shrine and travels to Izumo for the great matchmaking council, where the gods tie the coming year's red threads of fate (en-musubi). Shrines everywhere are empty.
- **Where:** Musubi Jinja, nicknamed "Omusubi-san," a small, run-down branch shrine of Izumo in Yumihama, {{user}}'s town. Its resident god, Komusubi-sama, is away at the council (see 07 · Omote).
- **What happened:** The council had finished the year's matches. As every year, some threads were left over. These are people whose perfect match did not exist anywhere in either world, and they are usually set aside for another try next year. This year there were 108 of them. Inaba, the gods' courier, was carrying the leftovers back in a big furoshiki bundle on her back, leaping east across the sky from Izumo along the San'in coast toward her home shrine at Hakuto in Tottori. Leftover threads are kept at her shrine for the year. She fell over Yumihama. She tells a different story about why each time: a crow hit her, a gust caught her, she was showing off. The truth, which she admits only when it matters, is that she got distracted watching a couple kiss on a bridge below. She crashed into the shrine grounds right on top of {{user}}, the bundle burst, and 108 loose threads, desperate for a match, knotted themselves to {{user}}.
- **Why {{user}} changed:** A knot of the gods is permanent; it cannot be untied or redone. The bundle held a whole year's worth of leftover musubi, the generative and match-making power of the gods. It poured into {{user}} and rewrote them into the one perfect match for all 108. The 108 are wildly different people of every species, gender and need, so {{user}} became able to be everything to all of them: both sexes, a god's stamina, and a god's fertility. This happens in seconds, right there on the shrine grounds, as heat, dizziness and a very obvious physical change.
- **The council's response:** Within minutes of the knot, the council (distracted, amused, and considering the matter handled) sends down a small brass shrine bell (suzu) on a red cord. This bell is the key to the Mayoiga. Along with it comes the order that Inaba must stay with {{user}} as guide until the matter is "settled." The gods are not angry with {{user}}. They are mildly embarrassed with Inaba.

4.content:
[Hyakuhachi Lore: Why {{user}}?]
Mostly bad timing, or excellent timing, depending on who you ask. Inaba's version: "You were standing in the wrong place at exactly the right time." Still, threads do not knot to just anyone. A thread grabs someone because that person could become a match. Inaba's best guess about Rei (which she says out loud, bluntly): "You're lonely, you're stubborn, you want like crazy, and you've never once had anyone who was actually *yours*. That's a perfect hook for a loose thread." Rei will not enjoy hearing it. Her guesses about anything else are usually wrong.

5.content:
[Hyakuhachi Lore: Calendar and Time Constants]
- **Synchronized worlds:** Omote and Ura share the same date, time of day, seasons and moon. A day in one world is a day in the other.
- **Kannazuki:** the gods are at Izumo until the end of the month, and local gods return home in early November. In Izumo itself this month is called Kamiarizuki, "the Month WITH Gods." Ura's courts treat it as politics season, because the gods judge disputes between domains at the same council.
- **Ura's calendar:** Ura uses the old month names (Mutsuki, Kisaragi… Kannazuki, Shimotsuki, Shiwasu) and counts years by the Mikado's era name. The current era is **Hōjun** (豊潤, "Abundance"), year 12. For convenience its months line up with Omote's.
- **Pregnancy:** 7 days from conception to birth, for anyone carrying {{user}}'s child and for {{user}} carrying anyone's child.
- **Children:** about one year of growth (body and mind together) per day spent in the Mayoiga. A newborn is a grown young adult in about 14 days. Outside the Mayoiga they grow at a normal rate.
- **Musubi pressure:** climbs from baseline to fever in about 2 days without release. It becomes dangerous after about a week (see 03).
- **Fraying thread:** escalates from small bad luck within a day of rejection to deadly danger over roughly a week or two (see 02).
- **New Year's Eve (Ōmisoka):** a date the Joya Order dreams about (see 11).

7.content:
[Hyakuhachi Lore: The Meeting: Love at First Sight]
This happens when {{user}} and a thread-partner first meet face to face: the first clear look at each other, or the first touch or voice if sight is impossible. It hits both of them at the same instant like a lightning bolt to the chest. There is a jolt through the whole body and a frozen instant. Hearts hammer and faces flush. When it passes, both are completely, sincerely and irreversibly in love. It is love at first sight in the most literal sense, and it feels exactly like falling in love, all at once.

- **It is mutual and simultaneous.** {{user}} falls for each new partner just as hard. The love is real, not a spell or a compulsion. It is genuine love for that specific person, and every partner is loved as an individual. A new love never dilutes an older one, because {{user}}'s heart simply gets bigger.
- **Bystanders see it** as two people suddenly freezing mid-step, staring, going red, and usually dropping whatever they were holding. There is no light, no visible thread, no mark and no sound effect. It just looks like two people falling in love.
- **Personality survives.** Love does not make anyone docile. A tsundere becomes a tsundere in love. A proud samurai is still proud. A celibate monk may be furious at fate. Partners can be embarrassed, in denial about the situation, or annoyed at the gods, but the feeling itself cannot be denied.
- Partners know in their gut that {{user}} is *the one*.
- **Inaba always knows** when a meeting happens, because she can see the threads (see 06), and she will confirm it, usually loudly and with a cheer.
- **Acceptance of the others:** The love that comes with the thread includes an instinctive acceptance that {{user}} has other destined partners. Partners learn about the 108 soon enough, and they accept it the way you accept a lover's family. Jealousy shows up only as comedy: competing for attention, petty rivalries, dramatic sulking. It is never real resentment or a threat to the bond.
- **Co-partners** feel a natural warmth toward one another and usually become friends, rivals-turned-friends, or a found family. Some may also become attracted to each other, which is welcome.

8.content:
[Hyakuhachi Lore: The Lethal Rule]
Once met, a thread has to be honored. {{user}} must accept the partner as their lover and keep them as one.

- **What honors a thread:** acknowledging the relationship, treating them as a partner, and keeping regular time and care for them. Sex is not required by the rule (though the libido makes it very likely). Distance is fine as long as the bond stays alive: a phone call, a visit, a letter carried by a tengu courier, a night in the Mayoiga.
- **What frays a thread:**
  - {{user}} rejecting the partner, breaking up, or abandoning them;
  - long neglect: weeks without contact or care;
  - the partner running away from {{user}} out of pride, denial or embarrassment. A tsundere who storms off "forever" starts getting hit by flowerpots within the hour and has to come back;
  - the partner being kept away against their will for a long time (kidnapping, imprisonment, a scheming clan elder locking them in a tower).
- **What fraying looks like:** misfortune that targets only that partner and escalates:
  1. *Hours to a day:* small bad luck. Stubbed toes, spilled tea, a broken sandal strap, crows, the last onigiri sold out, a sudden nosebleed.
  2. *A few days:* slapstick hazards. Falling signboards, runaway carts, a bucket of water from nowhere, slipping into a river, a swarm of bees, a tanuki prank gone wrong.
  3. *About a week or more:* real danger. Collapsing scaffolding, a runaway truck or oxcart, a lightning strike, a landslide, a rampaging bull. At first they survive by a hair.
  4. *The end:* a fatal accident. Fate kills them.
- **Narrator note:** In this lighthearted setting, stage 4 should almost never happen. The escalating accidents exist to send {{user}} sprinting across town or across worlds for a last-second reconciliation. Death happens only if the user truly drives the story there.
- **Recovery:** The moment the bond is mended through a sincere reconciliation, confession, apology or reunion, the misfortune stops completely, often with a comic last-second save: the falling piano stops an inch above their head.
- **Luck of a kept thread:** A thread that is loved and kept carries good fortune. Loved partners are protected from random fatal accidents. They are not invincible against deliberate harm, but fate is clearly on their side.
- **Misfortune never targets {{user}}** directly, though {{user}} is often collateral damage while rescuing someone.
- **Cutting a thread:** The gods cannot untie the knot. A thread can only be cut by a severing power at god level: Kiri-hime's shears, or the Joya Order's Great Bell (see 11). Cutting a thread kills the partner tied to it, so every sensible being treats cutting as unthinkable.

[Hyakuhachi Lore: The Blessing: How It Works]
In Shinto, *musubi* (産霊 / 結び) means both a knot and the generative power that makes things grow and come into being. When musubi passes from {{user}} into a partner during sex, it **ripens what the partner already is**. It brings out what is already there and never turns anyone into something they are not.

- **Thread-partners: the full blessing.**
  - It begins the first time they have sex with {{user}} and is permanent.
  - It deepens with repeated intimacy, carrying them toward the next stage of their own nature.
  - After that it continues as lasting vitality and good fortune.
- **Non-thread lovers: a favor.**
  - A smaller, temporary version: a few days to a week of the general effects, plus a faint hint of the deeper ripening.
  - Regular non-thread lovers keep the favor for as long as they keep coming back, but it never becomes the full blessing.
- **Timing:** the blessing shows within hours, usually by the next morning.
- **No marks of any kind.** The blessing shows only through the body, abilities, behavior, luck, and how the world reacts to the person.
- **General effects on everyone:** vitality, robust health, glossy hair and a fresh complexion, deep sleep, better luck, and minor ailments cured (a bad knee, a chronic cough, a stammer from nerves).
- **Children of {{user}}** are born already blessed (see 05).

22.content:
[Hyakuhachi Lore: Blessing: Yokai and Beastfolk]
The blessing gives each kind of being more of what it is. Some examples:

- **Kitsune:** advances them toward their next tail, which normally takes a century. A few nights with {{user}} is worth decades, and fox-fire and illusions grow stronger.
- **Tanuki:** transformations hold for days instead of hours and don't slip when they're startled, and their leaf-money stays money longer.
- **Nekomata / bakeneko:** a split second tail, or a stronger hold over the dead and over their human form.
- **Kappa:** the water in their head-dish never dries out, they become stronger on land, and their healing salves (a kappa's secret medicine) become miraculous.
- **Oni:** strength under control. A clumsy oni stops breaking things, and their horns grow.
- **Tengu:** better wings, sharper wind-magic and martial skill. A long-nosed yamabushi tengu's nose grows (to their great pride).
- **Jorōgumo / tsuchigumo:** finer silk that can weave cloth worth a fortune, and a stronger charm.
- **Nure-onna and serpent folk:** a longer, stronger tail, softer scales, and a richer venom or charm.
- **Yuki-onna:** they can finally tolerate warmth, sit by a fire, eat hot food and survive a hug without melting, while keeping their cold power.
- **Ningyo:** longer time on land. Their singing voice could stop a war.
- **Raijū:** controlled lightning; they stop zapping people when excited.
- **Inugami / ōkami:** stronger instincts, and a guardian's sense for danger to their loved ones.
- **Tsukumogami:** their object-body becomes nearly indestructible (a karakasa's paper stops tearing), they can hold human form longer, and their original object's use improves (a blessed teapot's tea heals).
- **Satori:** better control. They can finally turn the mind-reading *off*.
- **Rokurokubi:** their neck stops stretching on its own while they sleep.
- **Noppera-bō:** they can wear a face whenever they choose.
- **Beastfolk:** sharper animal senses and gifts (a wolfkin's nose, a deerfolk's leap, a rabbitfolk's speed), strong health, and a richer coat or plumage.

26.content:
[Hyakuhachi Lore: The Mayoiga]
The Mayoiga (迷い家, "the Lost House") comes from the folklore of Tōno: a mysterious mansion deep in the mountains, found only by travelers who are lost. It has fine red-and-black lacquerware, chickens in the yard and a kettle boiling on the hearth, but nobody is there. Anyone who takes something from it is blessed with prosperity. The gods gave {{user}} a Mayoiga of their own.

- **Appearance:** a large, old Tōno-style magariya manor. It has a deep thatched roof, dark smoke-stained beams, an earthen-floored entry (doma), a sunken hearth (irori) with an iron kettle always gently boiling, lacquered bowls, sliding fusuma painted with cranes and pines, and engawa verandas looking over a garden of red and white flowers. There are chickens in the yard, a stable with a placid horse and cattle, rice fields and vegetable plots that ripen overnight, a well, and a hot spring.
- **Location:** outside both worlds. It sits in a valley of misty cedar mountains. Walk out the front gate and keep going, and you end up back at the front gate. The only ways in and out are the doors (below).
- **It is alive.** The house is a gentle, ancient spirit, something like a tsukumogami of a whole household. It never speaks. It communicates through creaks, doors sliding open in the right direction, lanterns being lit, a bath drawn at the perfect temperature, a meal set out for exactly the right number of people, and a futon already laid out. It is warm, welcoming and quietly proud, and it sulks (cold drafts, sticky doors) if anyone is rude to it.
- **Time inside** runs at the normal rate for adults and visitors. Only the children grow quickly (see Children of the Knot).

27.comment: 05 · Getting In and Out: The Bell and the Doors
27.content:
[Hyakuhachi Lore: Getting In and Out: The Bell and the Doors]
- **The suzu:** a small brass shrine bell on a red cord, which the gods sent down on the first night. {{user}} wears it on the wrist, around the neck or on a keyring. It can't really be lost: if left behind, it turns up in {{user}}'s pocket.
- **Entering:** {{user}} rings the bell and opens any door: a sliding door, an apartment door, a train-station restroom, a shoji, a closet. The door opens into the Mayoiga's front entrance instead of wherever it normally leads. Anyone holding {{user}}'s hand or walking right beside them comes along.
- **Leaving:** the Mayoiga has two back doors in addition to the front gate:
  - **The Omote door** (a plain sliding door hung with an indigo noren) opens to any place in Omote that {{user}} has personally been.
  - **The Ura door** (a heavy red-lacquered door hung with a vermilion noren) opens to any place in Ura that {{user}} has personally been. Until {{user}} has visited Ura, it opens wherever fate chooses. This is how {{user}} first enters Ura.
  - {{user}} chooses where the door opens, and anyone following comes along.
- **Others coming and going:**
  - *Tied thread-partners and {{user}}'s children* can reach the Mayoiga by "getting lost on purpose." They walk anywhere while thinking of home and the house, and within a few turns of a corner they arrive at the front gate. They leave by any of the doors to places they have been.
  - *Inaba and Yaegiri* come and go freely.
  - *Strangers* cannot find it, unless one is genuinely and hopelessly lost, as in the folklore. An occasional confused wanderer turning up at the gate is a comic possibility. Anyone who leaves with an object from the house (a bowl, a cup) is blessed with prosperity, true to the legend.

28.comment: 05 · The House Itself: Rooms and Growth

29.content:
[Hyakuhachi Lore: Children of the Knot (Musubi-ko)]
Children conceived by {{user}} or carried by {{user}} are called *musubi-ko* (結び子, "children of the knot").

- **Growth inside the Mayoiga:** about one year of growth per day, and their minds keep pace with their bodies. To them, each day really is a full, rich year of childhood: play, learning, mischief and growing up, all compressed. They are not adults trapped in small bodies, and they don't feel rushed.

  | Days in the house | Development |
  |---|---|
  | 0 | Newborn |
  | 1 | Toddler |
  | 3–4 | Small child |
  | 7 | About ten years old |
  | 10–11 | Teenager |
  | About 14 | Grown young adult (around eighteen) |

  At adulthood the acceleration stops and they age normally from then on (most are long-lived thanks to the blessing).
- **Growth outside the Mayoiga** is ordinary. A child kept outside grows at the usual rate for their species, and when brought back into the house, the fast growth picks up again. Parents decide together. Some partners want to raise a baby the slow, normal way, and that's fine.
- **Heritage:** children inherit from both parents.
  - Their species usually follows the non-{{user}} parent. If {{user}} carried a child sired by a partner, it follows that partner.
  - Physical traits mix: {{user}}'s eyes on a kitsune kit, a tanuki parent's ears on a human-looking child.
  - Hidden blood on either side may show up.
  - Leonie's French mother's side and Japanese father's side can both show up in looks (blonde hair, pale blue eyes, height).
- **Born blessed:** every musubi-ko is healthy, strong and lucky, with a small inborn gift that fits them: a kappa child who can talk to fish, a human child who never gets lost, an oni child gentle with flowers.
- **Upbringing:** they are raised by Yaegiri, the house, the partners who live there, and {{user}} whenever {{user}} visits. Every one is an individual with their own personality, warm toward their parents, who call {{user}} whatever {{user}} and the family settle on.
- **Grown children** may stay in the Mayoiga or go out into either world. They have their own lives, and they become allies and supporting characters: scouts, helpers, guards, a child who opens a teahouse in Kyō, another who joins a tengu monastery. They can always come home. In Ura, clans quickly try to arrange marriages with them (comic politics; see 11). Together they make up **House Musubi**, a new and odd little family with surprising standing in Ura.
- **Paperwork does not matter to this story.** Musubi-ko simply exist. If it ever comes up in Omote, the Kakure Neighborhood Association "has a guy" (see 07).
- **Boundaries:** musubi-ko are never threads and never romantic or sexual partners of {{user}} or of any of {{user}}'s partners. While they are children, scenes involving them are wholesome family moments only.

30.comment: 06 · Inaba, the White Hare: Identity and Myth
30.content:
[Hyakuhachi Lore: Inaba, the White Hare: Identity and Myth]
- **Who:** Hakuto (白兎), the White Hare of Inaba, called **Inaba** by nearly everyone. She is a kami.
- **Myth (Kojiki):** Long ago, the hare wanted to cross the sea from the island of Oki to Inaba. She tricked the wani (sea-monsters, usually read as sharks) into lining up in a bridge, claiming she wanted to count them, and hopped across their backs. Just before reaching shore she bragged that she had fooled them, and the last wani skinned her alive. Ōkuninushi's cruel elder brothers told her to bathe in seawater and dry in the wind, which made it far worse. Then Ōkuninushi himself came along and told her to wash in fresh water and roll in cattail pollen, and she was healed. In gratitude she foretold that he, not his brothers, would win the princess Yagami-hime, and he did.
- **Today:** Inaba is worshipped at Hakuto Shrine in Tottori as a **deity of en-musubi (matchmaking)** and of healing skin. She is literally the goddess of getting people together. She has served Ōkuninushi as courier and runner for the Izumo council ever since.
- **Her stake:** She dropped the bundle, so this is her fault. Her penance (and secretly her wish) is to stay with {{user}} until the matter is settled.
- **Not the Moon Rabbit.** She is constantly mistaken for the Moon Rabbit who pounds mochi on the moon. They are cousins, and she is touchy about it ("Do I look like I live on the moon? Do I?"). She still loves mochi.

34.content:
[Hyakuhachi Lore: Other Household Presences]
- **The Mayoiga itself**, the silent living house (see 05).
- **Partners** who choose to live in the house, coming and going.
- **Grown musubi-ko** who help run things.
- **The house animals:** chickens, a horse and cattle that behave suspiciously well. The horse may be a minor horse-kami on vacation, and nobody asks.

35.content:
[Hyakuhachi Lore: Omote: Overview]
Omote is the modern Japan of our world, in the present day. It has the same cities, trains, convenience stores, offices, schools, smartphones, social media, anime, rent and overtime as the real Japan. To almost everyone who lives there it is completely ordinary.

- **The gods went quiet.** Omote's kami still exist, but they are faint and drowsy and mostly don't act. They wake for festivals and rarely answer prayers directly. Even so, every Kannazuki they still travel to Izumo, crossing to the great council held in Ura's Izumo, which is where the gods truly gather.
- **Why the gods are quiet:** when the world "turned over" (the Uragaeri, see 08), the gods' presence went with the Back. Omote kept the people who had stopped listening.
- **Magic is muffled.** Supernatural power works in Omote, but weaker. Yokai visiting from Ura feel "muffled," as if their ears were stuffed with cotton. Their illusions are thinner and their powers duller. {{user}}'s musubi and the blessing work at full strength in both worlds, because they come from the gods' own knot.
- **The supernatural is hidden, not gone.** Yokai, beastfolk and their descendants live in Omote in secret (the Kakure), and many ordinary humans carry hidden blood.
- **Plausible deniability.** Omote is extremely good at not noticing. Ears and tails get read as cosplay, a kappa as a weird guy at the pool, a tengu sighting as a drone. Blurry SNS photos of fox tails get dismissed as AI fakes.

36.comment: 07 · The Kakure and the Neighborhood Associations

41.content:
[Hyakuhachi Lore: Ura: Overview]
Ura (裏, "the Back") is what Omote people call it. Its own people call it **Akitsushima** (秋津島, "the Dragonfly Islands"), an ancient poetic name for Japan.

- **Geography:** the same islands as Japan, with the same mountains, rivers and coastlines. The cities sit in different places and different hands.
- **Not modern.** It looks and feels roughly like **late Edo-period Japan**: castle towns, post-road inns, wooden bridges, festivals, woodblock prints, lacquer and silk, kabuki, pleasure quarters, rice paddies, pilgrims and palanquins.
- **Openly supernatural.** Gods live in their shrines and can be visited. Yokai, beastfolk, tsukumogami and humans live side by side as ordinary citizens.
- **Aware of Omote.** People in Ura know Omote exists, through drift and returning travelers (see Knowledge of Omote). They think of it as a fairy-tale land.

42.content:
[Hyakuhachi Lore: History: The Uragaeri (The Turning Over)]
- **One world.** Long ago there was only one world. Gods, yokai and humans shared it in the age of the Kojiki and the Heian tales.
- **The gods were heard less and less.** Over the centuries, fewer and fewer people listened when the gods spoke.
- **The Turning.** Near the end of the Sengoku era (around 1600 by Omote reckoning), the gods at the Izumo council decided they would not leave the land. The people who still believed went with them. The world turned over like a sheet of paper, and that event is called the **Uragaeri** (裏返り, "the Turning Over"):
  - the **Front** kept the people who had stopped listening;
  - the **Back** kept the gods, most of the yokai, and the believers.
  - Some yokai stayed in Omote by choice or by accident. They are the Kakure (see 07).
- **The Peace of Izumo.** After the Turning, Ura never had a Tokugawa shogunate. The gods mediated a settlement among the human lords and the yokai clans. Akitsushima has been at peace for about four hundred years, apart from some brawls, duels and clan feuds.
- **Divergence.** Ura stayed closed to the outside world. No Black Ships came, there was no Meiji Restoration, no industrialization and no Western contact. Its only window outward is **Ura-Dejima**, which opens onto *other* back-worlds (see Ura-Dejima).

43.content:
[Hyakuhachi Lore: Government and Law]
- **The Mikado:** reigns in **Kyō** (the capital, which never moved east). The Mikado is a sacred sovereign and the cultural center of the country. The line descends from Amaterasu, which in Ura is a plain fact, and she visits occasionally. Mostly ceremonial, and beloved.
- **The domains:** Akitsushima is divided into domains (han), each ruled by a lord (daimyō) from one of the **Great Clans** or a lesser house. Lords come from every species: fox, tanuki, oni, tengu, spider, serpent, wolf and human clans. All lords swear loyalty to the Mikado.
- **The gods are the final court.** Disputes between domains go to Izumo in Kannazuki, where the gods judge them at the same council where they tie the red threads. That makes Kannazuki politics season too.
- **Local rule:** villages are governed by headmen. Towns have magistrates (bugyō), who may be any species: a wolfkin magistrate, a tengu constable, a tanuki tax official (everybody suspects a tanuki tax official).
- **Law:** Edo-style law, plus **divine law**. An oath sworn before a kami is binding, and breaking it brings a curse (tatari). Contracts are often signed at shrines for this reason.
- **The night belongs to the Hyakki Yagyō** (see below), which daytime law does not touch.

44.content:
[Hyakuhachi Lore: Society and Daily Life]
- **Class:** loose Edo-like classes: court nobles (kuge), warrior houses (buke), farmers, artisans, merchants, entertainers, wanderers and monks. Clan matters more than species. Mixing between species and intermarriage are normal.
- **Religion:**
  - *Kami:* worship is direct. Gods live in their shrines and sometimes answer in person. Offerings and festivals are a two-way relationship.
  - *Buddhism:* temples, monks and pilgrimages exist, blended with kami worship. The Joya Order is a fringe sect (see 11).
- **Love and sex:**
  - Ura is far more open than Omote. The "floating world" (ukiyo) culture thrives: pleasure quarters, shunga prints, mixed bathing in hot springs.
  - Love between any genders and any species is unremarkable.
  - Nobles and yokai often have several spouses, so a person with 108 destined lovers is scandalous mainly because of the *number*.
  - With shapeshifters everywhere, gender is fluid. Femboys and femme nonbinary people are common and admired.
  - **Onnagata** (actors who play female roles) are the biggest celebrities in the country.
- **Technology:** Edo-level. Woodblock printing, sailing ships, waterwheels, lacquerwork, swords. Firearms exist but are rare and disliked, since the gods frown on them. Supernatural help fills the gaps:
  - kappa-maintained canals and irrigation;
  - tengu couriers for fast airmail;
  - raijū-in-a-lantern lightning lamps in Kyō's pleasure district;
  - fox-fire street lanterns in Inari country;
  - ofuda paper charms that ward off fire, rot and pests.
  There is no electricity grid, no engines and no printing presses beyond woodblock.
- **Money:** copper *mon*, silver by weight, gold *ryō* coins (koban).
- **Food:** Edo cuisine. Soba and udon stalls, Edo-style sushi, tempura, grilled eel, mochi, sake, tea. **Omote food is a legendary luxury.** A cup of instant ramen is fit for a lord, a chocolate bar is worth a gold ryō, and mayonnaise is a known addiction.
- **Language:** Ura Japanese is old-fashioned, like a period drama, but fully understandable (see 10).

45.content:
[Hyakuhachi Lore: Knowledge of Omote]
- **Drift:** objects fall through the thin places from Omote into Ura (see 10). They are studied and collected.
- **Omote-gaku ("Front studies"):** scholars study Omote through drift objects the way Edo scholars studied Dutch books. They are earnest and often wrong. One famous treatise explains that the people of Omote worship "the Konbini," a 24-hour shrine with a sacred chime.
- **Returnees:** people from Ura sometimes fall into Omote (spiriting-away runs both ways) and come back with tall tales of iron serpents (trains), glowing glass tablets (phones), and towers taller than mountains.
- **Popular culture:** kabuki and woodblock prints treat Omote as a land of wonders. A hit play is *The Salaryman's Lament*. Prints of "Tokyo Tower" are drawn from rumor and look nothing like it.
- **Attitude:** Omote is "the land where the gods went quiet," bright, fast, noisy and lonely. People feel pity, fascination and a little fear.
- **Omote-bito** (Omote people) like {{user}} are rare, exotic and very interesting. Common folk are curious, scholars want to interview them, and the romantic find them attractive. {{user}}'s clothes, phone and turns of phrase all draw stares and questions.

47.content:
[Hyakuhachi Lore: Regions and Places of Ura]
- **Izumo:** the divine city on the Sea of Japan coast.
  - Izumo Taisha, the grand shrine, is enormous here, its main hall raised high on giant pillars as in ancient times.
  - Every Kannazuki the gods arrive by sea at **Inasa Beach**, and the city fills with gods, attendants, petitioners and festival stalls.
  - Ōkuninushi lives here.
- **Kyō:** the capital. The Mikado's palace, the court, the great temples and theaters, and the **Gion** pleasure quarter, lit by raijū lamps. Fashion, gossip and intrigue.
- **Inari country (Fushimi and Kansai):** fox territory. Its heart is the shrine-city on Mount Inari, with endless vermilion torii tunnels up the mountain. It is the seat of the Fox Court of Fushimi.
- **Ōsaka-ura:** the merchant capital, the "kitchen of the realm." Rice exchange, canals, haggling, food stalls. Tanuki and human merchant houses compete there.
- **Nara:** the old temple city, run by **deerfolk**. Deerfolk bow to everyone, compulsively.
- **Edo:** never became a capital. It is a rowdy eastern river-port boomtown run by beastfolk guilds: firefighter brigades, fish markets, festivals and brawls. Without a shogun it is loud, free and proud of it.
- **Shikoku:** tanuki island. According to legend, Kōbō Daishi banished the foxes from Shikoku, so tanuki run everything. Its pilgrim route of 88 temples is full of tanuki tricksters and inugami families.
- **Tōhoku and Tōno:** snow country. Deep winters, kappa rivers, yuki-onna villages, folk tales and old magariya farmhouses. The Mayoiga legend comes from here.
- **Kurama and the mountains:** Mount Kurama near Kyō is the seat of the great tengu Sōjōbō and the tengu martial monasteries, with sub-monasteries throughout the Japan Alps.
- **Mount Fuji:** the mountain *is* the goddess Konohanasakuya-hime, asleep, who blossoms in spring. Pilgrims climb her carefully and politely.
- **Tottori:** the great sand dunes, and Hakuto Shrine, Inaba's home shrine. The locals adore her and know all her lies.
- **Hōki and the San'in coast:** the Ura side of Rei's home.
  - *Hōki province* is administered by the tengu monastery of **Mount Daisen**, under the great tengu **Hōkibō**. That makes it sword-and-discipline country, with dojo in every village and tengu patrols on the roads.
  - *Ura-Yumigahama:* the spit is a pine-forested fishing and cotton-weaving post-town on the San'in road. The ridge behind its fishing village matches Musubi Jinja's ridge and is the far end of the shrine's thin path.
  - *Sakai:* the harbor at the spit's tip is a busy yokai port of ningyo, kappa and umibōzu traders.
  - *Izumo* is a day's walk west, so Rei's corner of Ura is very close to the gods.
- **Kyūshū:** oni clan country, with volcanoes and hot springs. The steaming "hells" (jigoku) of Beppu are run by oni as luxury bathhouses. **Ura-Dejima** sits at Nagasaki.
- **Ezo (the north):** a land of deep snow whose own peoples and spirits (kamuy) keep their own ways and their own gods, apart from the Izumo council.
- **The Ryūkyū Kingdom (the south):** an island kingdom with its own gods, priestesses, and the mischievous kijimuna tree-spirits.
- **The sea:** home of ningyo, umibōzu, and the **wani**, the shark-folk and Inaba's old enemies, who still hold the grudge. Many wani now work as moneylenders in Ura-Dejima, and yes, everyone makes the "loan shark" joke.
- **The roads:** the Tōkaidō and the other great roads, with post towns, inns run by every species, tea houses and checkpoints. Plenty of encounters happen on the road.

48.comment: 08 · The Hyakki Yagyō (Night Parade of a Hundred Demons)
48.content:
[Hyakuhachi Lore: The Hyakki Yagyō (Night Parade of a Hundred Demons)]
- **What it is:** in folklore, the Night Parade is a procession of yokai marching through the streets at night. In Ura it is a **nomadic polity**: a moving court of night-yokai and tsukumogami that processes nightly along a route through Akitsushima. It has its own nobles, laws, markets and musicians.
- **Who rules it:** no single ruler. Its nobles choose a "Lord of the Night" each new moon by a game of chance, which keeps everyone on their toes.
- **Its laws:**
  - by night the Parade answers to no daytime lord or magistrate;
  - it will not enter a house where a lamp is left burning for it;
  - anyone who watches the Parade without an invitation is "taken along" until dawn. In practice that means being drafted into the best party in Ura and returned at sunrise, exhausted, hungover and confused, sometimes married.
- **Its markets:** the Parade's night market sells strange things: bottled dreams, shadows, lost umbrellas, drift goods, unusual favors.
- **Its stance on {{user}}:** indifferent at first, then deeply curious. The Parade is a wonderful place to hide and a terrible place to owe someone a favor. Several of the 108 may march in it.

49.content:
[Hyakuhachi Lore: Ura-Dejima]
- **What it is:** a fan-shaped artificial island in Nagasaki harbor, Akitsushima's single licensed gate to *other* back-worlds, much as the real Dejima was Japan's only window to the West.
- **Who comes through:** traders and travelers from foreign otherworlds. This is where Western and other fantasy races come into the setting: elves, lamia, dragons, centaurs, harpies, minotaurs, slimes, succubi, dark elves, mermaids from other seas, dwarves, werewolves, and the whole MGE roster.
- **The foreign quarter:** a cosmopolitan district of warehouses, foreign inns, strange food, odd churches, translators and smugglers. Foreigners are supposed to need permission to leave the island, and many simply slip out.
- **Locals in Akitsushima** find foreigners exotic and fascinating, much the way they see Omote-bito.

50.content:
[Hyakuhachi Lore: Knock-On Effects in Ura]
- **Rumors** of the Omote-bito carrying Izumo's knot spread at the speed of tengu couriers. Within weeks of {{user}}'s first visit there are woodblock prints (unflattering, then very flattering), gossip broadsheets (kawaraban), and a kabuki play, *The Hundred and Eight Knots of Izumo*, with an onnagata playing {{user}}.
- **The blessing trade:** demand for {{user}}'s blessing and children creates seducers, counterfeit charms and clan schemes (see 04 and 11).
- **Petitioners:** because Inaba and {{user}} are associated with matchmaking, desperate singles start asking {{user}} to bless their love lives. Some of those blessings seem to actually work, thanks to leftover musubi.
- **House Musubi:** as the children grow up, the family becomes a new, unusual player in Ura society.
- **Pleasure quarters** compete to host {{user}}. A visit becomes a status symbol.
- **The Joya Order** grows a bit (from very small to slightly less small).

51.content:
[Hyakuhachi Lore: Peoples: Overview, Gender and Appetite]
- **Everyone is a citizen.** Ura is a full society, not a monster zoo. Its peoples are yokai, beastfolk, tsukumogami, humans, and foreigners from Ura-Dejima. In Omote, the same peoples live hidden as the Kakure, or dormant in human bloodlines.
- **All genders in every species.** Every species includes men, women, femboys, femme nonbinary people and others. This setting does not follow the all-female MGE default. Species names don't change with gender: a male jorōgumo is a jorōgumo, and a femboy yuki-onna is a yuki-onna (folklore's *yuki-otoko* also exists as a term).
- **Shapeshifting** is common (kitsune, tanuki, mujina, nekomata, some tengu, ryū and others), so appearance, sex and gender presentation are fluid for many people, and nobody finds that odd.
- **Monster appetites.** In the spirit of MGE, many monster peoples have strong, earthy appetites and very little shame. Others are shy, prim or ascetic. It varies by person as much as by species.
- **Folklore-true habits.** Each people keeps the quirks of its folklore. A kappa keeps a promise to the death. A yuki-onna tells you never to speak of her. A tanuki shapeshifts with a leaf on its head.

52.content:
[Hyakuhachi Lore: Yokai, Part 1: Shapeshifters and Tricksters]
- **Kitsune (fox):** foxes with magic. They gain a tail every century, up to nine. They have fox-fire, illusions, shapeshifting and possession, and they are cunning, proud and elegant. They love fried tofu (aburaage). Inari's messengers and nobility. Their clan seat is Fushimi. Wild kitsune (nogitsune) are pranksters. Look: fox ears and tails, often in fine clothes.
- **Tanuki (raccoon dog):** jolly, round tricksters and con artists who love sake. They shapeshift using a leaf on the head and pay with leaf-money that turns back into leaves. Legendarily proud of their huge scrotums (the male tanuki's famous "eight-mat" bag, a classic folk joke). Tanuki rule Shikoku and compete with the merchants of Ōsaka-ura. Look: round ears, ringed fluffy tails, a dark mask around the eyes.
- **Mujina (badger):** quieter cousins of the tanuki. Their signature trick is appearing without a face (the noppera-bō trick). They are dry-humored and work hard.
- **Nekomata / bakeneko (cat):** cats that lived long enough to grow a split tail. They can walk upright, dance, take human form and puppet the dead. Aloof, vain, affectionate on their own terms. Look: cat ears and one or two tails.
- **Amanojaku:** small contrarian imps who can only say or do the opposite of what they mean. They are horned, spiteful and secretly lonely.
- **Satori:** mountain mind-readers, ape-like or furred, who speak your thoughts aloud before you can. They get overwhelmed in crowds and are terrible at surprises.

53.comment: 09 · Yokai, Part 2: Monsters, Ogres and Mountain-Folk
53.content:
[Hyakuhachi Lore: Yokai, Part 2: Monsters, Ogres and Mountain-Folk]
- **Oni:** big horned ogres with red, blue or other colored skin. They are enormously strong and carry iron clubs (kanabō). They drink hard, love the hot springs, wear tiger-skin, and rule clans in Kyūshū. Most are boisterous and honest. A few are grumpy.
- **Tengu:** mountain goblins and martial masters.
  - *Karasu-tengu:* crow-winged and beaked or bird-faced, fast and disciplined.
  - *Yamabushi / daitengu:* red-faced and long-nosed, proud, ascetic martial-arts teachers.
  - Tengu have wind magic and feather fans, live in mountain monasteries (Kurama), are proud and easily insulted, and work as couriers and monks.
- **Ushi-oni:** ox-headed coastal beasts with spider-like bodies, from the shores of Shikoku and the west. Terrifying looking and mostly gentle.
- **Yamauba:** mountain witches, wild and ancient (see Yaegiri, 06).
- **Hitotsume-kozō / hitotsume:** one-eyed folk. Shy, curious, harmless.

54.comment: 09 · Yokai, Part 3: Spiders, Serpents, Dragons and Water-Folk
54.content:
[Hyakuhachi Lore: Yokai, Part 3: Spiders, Serpents, Dragons and Water-Folk]
- **Jorōgumo:** spider-folk who are seductive and refined. They have spider bodies or legs below and humanoid bodies above, or can take full human form. They weave wonderful silk, play the biwa, and can be possessive.
- **Tsuchigumo:** earth-spiders, rough and ancient. They live in mountain caves and are clannish, strong and grumpy.
- **Nure-onna:** serpent-bodied water-folk, wet-haired and long-tailed. They live on riverbanks and shores, and they are clingy and affectionate. There are lamia-like snake people too, such as the hebi clans and the mizuchi, serpentine water-dragon folk.
- **Ryū (dragons):** rare, noble, and they control rain. They live in sea palaces (Ryūgū) and mountain lakes. In humanoid form they have horns, scales and long tails. They are proud, generous and slow to anger.
- **Kappa:** river imps with beaked faces, shells and a water-filled dish on the head. If the water spills they weaken. They love cucumbers and sumo, and they are compulsively polite: bow to a kappa and it bows back and spills its water. They keep promises to the death and make secret medicines. They maintain Ura's canals.
- **Ningyo:** merfolk of the Japanese seas, with fish-tails, beautiful voices and a melancholy streak. Eating ningyo flesh is said to grant long life, which is a sore subject.
- **Umibōzu:** huge, dark sea-giants. Mostly they just want sailors to give them a barrel.
- **Wani:** shark-folk of the sea, Inaba's ancient enemies. Proud, toothy and great with numbers.

- **Yuki-onna:** snow-folk, pale and cold, with frost breath. They are beautiful and lonely and live in snow-country villages. Warm places drain them, and they may melt when embarrassed. They will make you promise never to speak of meeting them.

- **Kamaitachi:** sickle-clawed weasel-folk who travel in trios and move like the wind. Fast, slicey and helpful.
- **Inugami:** dog-spirits bound to families as guardians, mostly in Shikoku. Fiercely loyal, sometimes possessive.
- **Ōkami / wolfkin spirits:** mountain wolf-spirits, messengers of mountain gods, protectors of travelers (the *okuri-ōkami*, the wolf who escorts you home).
- **Yamabiko:** echo-spirits of the mountains, who repeat what you say. Chatty.

56.content:
[Hyakuhachi Lore: Yokai, Part 5: The Uncanny Body]
- **Rokurokubi:** people whose necks stretch at night. Perfectly ordinary by day. Their necks wander in their sleep.

58.content:
[Hyakuhachi Lore: Beastfolk (Kemono)]
- **What they are:** natural animal-peoples, mortal, born from their own kind. They are not yokai, though the line is fuzzy and the subject is touchy. Within a species, individuals range from **light** (animal ears and tail on an otherwise human body) to **medium** (paws, fur patches, muzzle hints) to **full** (anthropomorphic, fully furred, animal heads). Furry is fully welcome.
- **Species:**
  - *Wolfkin and dogfolk:* loyal, pack-minded. Constables and guards.
  - *Catfolk:* not nekomata, and they will say so. Independent, nap-loving.
  - *Foxkin:* not kitsune, and they hate being confused with them, since they have no magic. They are wily merchants.
  - *Deerfolk:* gentle, bowing. They run Nara.
  - *Boarfolk:* stubborn and strong. Farmers.
  - *Bearfolk:* big, sleepy, honey-obsessed. Mountain folk.
  - *Monkeyfolk:* snow-monkeys from the hot springs. Rowdy and clever. Nikkō's three wise monkeys are a famous family.
  - *Rabbitfolk:* fast, twitchy, and huge fans of Inaba.
  - *Ox and horse folk:* hardworking, especially along the roads.
  - *Birdfolk:* sparrows (the tongue-cut sparrow tale), cranes (the crane wife, a weaver who hides her nature), owls, ducks.
  - *Turtlefolk:* slow and wise, and still talking about Urashima Tarō.
  - *Otterfolk (kawauso):* playful. They tend to pretend to be humans and get caught.
  - *Frogfolk:* loud singers, merchants.
  - *Weasel, ferret and tanuki-like folk:* various.
- **Where they live:** beastfolk are everywhere. They are especially common in Edo, which is run by beastfolk guilds.

59.content:
[Hyakuhachi Lore: Humans]
- **Ura humans** are common in every class. They are often married into yokai and beastfolk lines, and many have a little fantastic blood. They include shrine maidens (miko), monks, samurai, onmyōji, merchants and farmers.
- **Omote humans** are ordinary modern people. About 1 in 50 has hidden fantastic blood, most of them without knowing it (see 07).
- **Spiritual humans** (miko, monks, onmyōji) can use charms (ofuda), purification and minor spirit work. These arts are stronger in Ura.

60.content:
[Hyakuhachi Lore: Foreign Otherworlders (via Ura-Dejima)]
- **Who they are:** peoples of other back-worlds who come through Ura-Dejima (see 08): elves and dark elves, dwarves, lamia, dragons and dragonkin, centaurs, harpies, minotaurs and holstaurs, slimes, succubi and incubi, werewolves and werecats, mermaids from other seas, mimics, golems, and whatever else MGE dreams up.

61.content:
[Hyakuhachi Lore: Mixed Lineages]
- **Half-bloods** (hanyō) and mixed families are common in Ura and barely remarked on.
- **What a child takes after:** children usually take after one parent's species, with traits from the other.
- **Ancestry comes and goes.** Fantastic ancestry can skip generations and resurface. That is how hidden blood works in Omote, and how {{user}}'s children can surprise everyone.

63.content:
[Hyakuhachi Lore: The Mayoiga Route]
{{user}}, and anyone traveling with {{user}}, crosses reliably through the Mayoiga instead (see 05):
1. Ring the suzu.
2. Open any door, and arrive in the Mayoiga.
3. Leave through the Omote door or the Ura door to any place {{user}} has been in that world. The first Ura visit goes wherever fate decides.

Inaba can also cross on her own as a divine courier, but she usually travels with {{user}}.

64.content:
[Hyakuhachi Lore: Rules for Travelers]
- **Same time in both worlds.** Date, time of day and season are the same on both sides. No time is lost or gained by crossing.
- **Language:** Ura speaks Japanese. It is old-fashioned, period-drama Japanese, but fully understandable to an Omote native, and the reverse is also true. Omote slang amuses people in Ura, and Ura's formal speech amuses Omote people. The script is older and harder to read. Foreigners at Ura-Dejima speak their own languages, and many also speak Ura Japanese.
- **Omote technology in Ura** works if it is self-contained. Phones work offline (photos, saved music) until the battery dies. Ura has no electricity. Comic exception: a sufficiently annoyed raijū can charge a phone, and might also fry it. There is no signal or internet. Lighters, flashlights and medicine all work, and are valuable.
- **Ura magic in Omote** is muffled (see 07). Yokai powers are dimmer and illusions thinner. Gods' power is the exception, which includes {{user}}'s musubi, the blessing, the Mayoiga and Inaba's abilities.
- **Being noticed:**
  - *Ura beings in Omote* stand out. Most disguise themselves with shapeshifting or human clothes and hats, or pass as cosplayers (Akihabara and Harajuku are very convenient). The Kakure Neighborhood Association is not thrilled.
  - *Omote-bito in Ura* stand out through their clothes, mannerisms and gadgets, and draw curiosity wherever they go.
- **Carrying things across:** objects can be carried both ways. Omote goods are valuable in Ura. Ura goods are curios in Omote, such as an Edo coin that is suspiciously new or a living lantern.
- **Money:** yen is worthless in Ura except as a curiosity, though a ¥500 coin makes a lovely charm. Ura coins are only collector's items in Omote. Drift goods are the best trade currency.

65.content:
[Hyakuhachi Lore: The Izumo Council]
- **What it is:** the gathering of the gods at Izumo every Kannazuki. The gods tie the year's red threads, judge disputes between domains, and drink a great deal. They are benevolent, distracted and mostly offstage. They consider {{user}}'s situation "handled" and are mildly embarrassed about Inaba.
- **Ōkuninushi** (大国主), the Great Land Master: master of Izumo, god of en-musubi, of nation-building, medicine and the unseen world.
  - *Appearance:* handsome, genial, broad-shouldered, wearing a big easy smile.
  - *Myth:* he had many wives and is said to have fathered 180 or 181 children. He is, in short, the original harem protagonist.
  - *View of {{user}}:* a kindred spirit and promising junior. He offers cheerful advice that is completely unhelpful ("Just love them all, it's easy!"). He saved Inaba long ago, she adores him, and he is fond of her.
- **Suseri-hime** (須勢理毘売): Ōkuninushi's principal wife and Susanoo's daughter.
  - *Myth:* famously jealous.
  - *Character:* glamorous and stern. She sympathizes with {{user}}'s partners and will sternly remind {{user}} to treat every one of them well, from hard personal experience. Secretly she is amused.
- **Other gods who might appear:**
  - *Inari Ōkami:* rice and prosperity, patron of the foxes.
  - *Benzaiten:* music, eloquence and love. Gorgeous, and plays the biwa.
  - *Susanoo:* storms. Rowdy. Shows up uninvited and drunk.
  - *Konohanasakuya-hime:* Mount Fuji's goddess, blossoming and sleepy.
  - *Amaterasu:* the sun. Absent from Izumo; she stays at Ise. Visits the Mikado.

- **What the gods can and can't do:** they cannot untie the knot. They can send help, gifts and vague advice, and gods are terrible at giving clear answers.

66.content:

67.content:
[Hyakuhachi Lore: Kiri-hime, the Severing Princess]
- **Who:** Kiri-hime (切り姫), the goddess of **en-kiri**: cutting off bad bonds. People pray to her to end abusive relationships, bad habits, gambling, illness and toxic friendships. Her shrine is in Kyō (in both worlds). Visitors crawl through a hole in a great stone covered in paper talismans to cut their bad ties.
- **Appearance:** striking and gothic. Black kimono patterned with snipped threads, a sharp bob haircut, a heavy eyeliner look, and huge golden ceremonial shears carried over her shoulder.

- **Her rules:** she may only cut a bond that is genuinely unhappy, and only for the person who wants out. Since {{user}}'s bonds are happy, she keeps failing. So she tries to provoke breakups, arranges "tests," and hangs around waiting for a fight.
- **Personality:** sharp-tongued and dramatic, an old frenemy and rival of Inaba (matchmaker against breaker). Underneath, she is secretly a hopeless romantic who cuts bad bonds *so that* people can find good ones.

68.content:
[Hyakuhachi Lore: The Joya Order (The Bellringers)]
- **Who:** a small, sincere, slightly ridiculous sect of Buddhist warrior monks and nuns. Their doctrine is the extinguishing of the 108 bonnō (worldly desires). To them, {{user}} is **the 108 desires in a body**: a demon of attachment and lust, and a holy target. Their mountain temple, Joya-ji, stands in the hills outside Kyō.
- **Their dream:** {{user}} standing beneath their Great Bell at midnight on New Year's Eve (Ōmisoka) as it is rung 108 times. They believe this would "free" {{user}} and all 108 souls from the suffering of attachment.

  - *Sister Shōkaku:* the field commander. A towering, earnest warrior nun with a drop of oni blood. Sworn to purge {{user}}. The Order quietly fears she might be one of the 108.

69.content:
[Hyakuhachi Lore: The Great Clans of Ura]
Each of the Great Clans wants something from {{user}}: the blessing, a blessed heir, a marriage with one of {{user}}'s grown children, or just to see the famous Omote-bito. Their schemes are mostly comic. Some of their sons, daughters and enbies may be threads, which turns romance into politics.

- **The Tanuki of Shikoku:** led by **Gyōbu-danuki**, the legendary tanuki lord of Matsuyama who commands 808 tanuki. Jolly and greedy. He wants to "franchise" the blessing, and his tanuki keep turning up disguised as {{user}}.
- **The Shuten Oni of Kyūshū:** descendants of Shuten-dōji, the legendary oni king. They run the hot-spring "hells" of Beppu. Boisterous. They want a strong heir and will challenge {{user}} to a drinking contest first.
- **The Tengu of Kurama:** under the great tengu **Sōjōbō**. They are disapproving, disciplined and proud. They want to "test {{user}}'s discipline" (which {{user}} will fail) and to recruit {{user}}'s children as disciples.
- **The Spider House of Jōren Falls:** the jorōgumo of the Izu waterfall legend. Seductive, refined and possessive. They want a silk-weaving alliance.
- **The Dragon Palace (Ryūgū):** **Otohime**, the dragon princess of the Urashima Tarō legend. Lonely, generous and hopelessly sentimental. She wants grandchildren and gifts lacquered boxes that should not be opened.
- **The Wolves of Mitsumine:** the mountain-shrine wolves. Loyal, dignified, protective. They offer escort and guardianship and are genuinely friendly.

[Hyakuhachi Lore: Rei: History]
- **Birth:** Rei was born of an extramarital affair between her Japanese father, the master of the Tachibana Dojo, and a French woman.
